title: From Problem to Program
summary: The unit shows how problems can be described using functions (Funktionen) and precise algorithms (Algorithmen). The Euclidean algorithm (Euklidischer Algorithmus) is used to explain recursion (Rekursion), the base case (Rekursionsanker), and termination (Termination). It then introduces key MiniJava constructs such as variables (Variablen), assignments (Wertzuweisungen), input/output (Eingabe/Ausgabe), selection (Selektion), blocks (Blöcke), and iteration (Iteration).
keyFacts: Arithmetic operations can be modeled as functions, for example, addition as $f: Q \times Q \to Q$.
An algorithm is a precise description of how to produce a desired result from an input.
An algorithm also describes a sequence of individual process steps and can process or implement a function.
Not every function is computable; this question belongs to computability theory.
The Euclidean algorithm finds the greatest common divisor of two positive integers $a$ and $b$.
If $a=b$, the base case is reached and the algorithm returns $a$.
If $a>b$, $a$ is replaced by $a-b$ and the algorithm returns to step 1.
If $a<b$, $b$ is replaced by $b-a$ and the algorithm returns to step 1.
The Euclidean algorithm terminates because the values remain positive and the base case is eventually reached.
Static finiteness means that the description of an algorithm has finite length.
Dynamic finiteness is associated with termination of the execution.
Variables have values that can be used as arguments for operations.
Variables declared inside `main` are not given a default value and must be defined.
An assignment changes the value stored in a variable.
MiniJava is used for the first exercises and at the beginning of the module.
`readInt` is used to input an integer, and `write` is used to output a value.
`if`/`else` enables conditional selection; blocks group statements, and iteration means repeated execution.
Comments can explain a program; `javac` compiles it and `java` runs it.

review.notes: 44 Fragen geprüft. Eine Cloze-Frage hatte mit „1“ einen nicht eindeutig falschen Distraktor, da der Wert bei bestimmten Eingaben tatsächlich 1 sein kann; dieser wurde durch $a+1$ ersetzt. Keine Fragen mussten entfernt werden.

questions.prompt: Which description applies to an algorithm?

options.text: A single value stored in a variable.
A precise description of how to produce a desired result from an input.
A list of all possible functions, regardless of their input.
A random sequence of outputs without specified steps.

questions.explanation: An algorithm specifies precisely how to produce a desired result from an input. To do so, it describes a sequence of individual process steps.

questions.prompt: A function is to take two rational numbers as input and output their sum as a rational number. Here, $\mathbb{Q}$ denotes the set of rational numbers, $\mathbb{N}_{>0}$ the positive natural numbers, and $\times$ an ordered pair of numbers. Which signature describes this function?

options.text: $f: \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}$
$f: \mathbb{N}_{>0} \to \{yes,no\}$
$f: \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}$
$f: \{yes,no\} \to \mathbb{N}_{>0}$

questions.explanation: The function receives a pair of rational numbers and returns their sum. Therefore, its domain is $\mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}$ and its codomain is $\mathbb{Q}$.
concepts: Input and output sets (Eingabe- und Ausgabemenge)

questions.prompt: Which statements describe an algorithm? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: It consists of a sequence of individual process steps.
Every mathematically described function is automatically computable.
It can compute or implement a function $f$.
It precisely describes how a desired result is produced from an input.

questions.explanation: An algorithm links an input, a desired result, and a precise sequence of process steps. However, it is not true that every function is computable.

questions.prompt: Every function is computable.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Not every function is computable. This limitation is studied in computability theory.

questions.prompt: In the Euclidean algorithm, when $a=b$ is reached, $\gcd(a,b)=___$.

options.text: a-b
a
a+b

questions.explanation: When $a=b$, the base case is reached; the algorithm stops and returns $a$.

questions.prompt: What is the base case of the Euclidean algorithm?

options.text: $a=b$
$a<b$
$a>b$

questions.explanation: The base case is the condition $a=b$. No further computation is performed then; the current value is returned.

questions.prompt: What happens in the recursion step when $a>b$?

options.text: $a$ is replaced by $a-b$, and the algorithm returns to step 1.
The algorithm immediately returns $b$.
$b$ is replaced by $b-a$, and the algorithm stops.
1 is added to both $a$ and $b$.

questions.explanation: When $a>b$, the larger value $a$ is replaced by the positive difference $a-b$. The check then starts again at step 1.

questions.prompt: What does static finiteness mean for an algorithm?

options.text: Every function can be computed by the algorithm.
All variables always have positive values.
Every step is executed infinitely many times.
The description of the algorithm has finite length.

questions.explanation: Static finiteness concerns the description itself: it has finite length.

questions.prompt: Dynamic finiteness refers to the completion of an execution.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: In this material, dynamic finiteness is associated with termination, that is, the end of an execution.

questions.prompt: A variable declared inside `main` can be used safely without being defined first.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Variables inside `main` are not given a default value. They must be defined before they are used.
`x` receives the value 3. The assignment then computes $3+19=22$, and `write` outputs 22.

questions.prompt: What value does the Euclidean algorithm return for $a=18$ and $b=12$?
questions.explanation: First, $18$ is replaced by $18-12=6$. Then $12$ is replaced by $12-6=6$; when $a=b=6$, the algorithm ends.

questions.prompt: After `x = 7; result = x;`, `result` has the value 7, while `x` remains unchanged.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The current value of `x` is stored in `result`. Assigning to `result` does not change `x`.
The condition $4>9$ is false, so the `else` branch runs. It computes $9-4=5$.

questions.prompt: Which mapping matches the MiniJava commands?

options.text: `readInt` outputs a value, and `write` reads an integer.
Both commands declare variables.
Both commands repeat part of a program.
`readInt` reads an integer, and `write` outputs a value.

questions.explanation: `readInt` is for input, while `write` is for output. They therefore have different roles in a program.

questions.prompt: What is conditional selection using `if` and `else` called?

options.text: Selection
Comment
Assignment
Iteration

questions.explanation: In selection, a condition determines which branch is executed. `if` and `else` provide this kind of conditional choice.

questions.prompt: What value does the Euclidean algorithm return for $a=15$ and $b=6$?
questions.explanation: Since $15>6$, $a$ becomes 9 and then 3. Next, $b$ becomes $6-3=3$; the base case returns 3.

questions.prompt: In the Euclidean algorithm, after replacing the larger value, the process returns to step 1.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: After replacing $a$ when $a>b$ or replacing $b$ when $a<b$, the process continues at step 1.

options.text: The final assignment changes `x` to 26.
`result` has the value 26.
`x` has the value 7.
`result` remains 7 permanently.

questions.explanation: `x` remains 7, while the final assignment uses the current value of `x` and sets `result` to $7+19=26$.

questions.prompt: Which order is correct for compiling and running a MiniJava program?

options.text: First run with `java`, then compile with `javac`.
First output variables, then describe the algorithm.
First compile with `write`, then run with `readInt`.
First compile with `javac`, then run with `java`.

questions.explanation: The process described is to compile with `javac` and then run with `java`.

questions.prompt: `if`/`else` chooses a branch based on a condition and is therefore a form of ___.

options.text: Comment
Selection
Assignment
Iteration

questions.explanation: Selection chooses between possible execution paths based on a condition.

questions.prompt: What are blocks used for in MiniJava?

options.text: They make every function computable.
They replace all variables with default values.
They group statements, for example in `if` or loop statements.
They automatically read an integer.

questions.explanation: Blocks group several statements together. This lets statements belong together in an `if` branch or a loop.

questions.prompt: What value does the Euclidean algorithm return for $a=48$ and $b=18$?
questions.explanation: The values evolve as $(48,18)\to(30,18)\to(12,18)\to(12,6)\to(6,6)$. The base case returns 6.

questions.prompt: Which observations explain why the Euclidean algorithm terminates? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: The values of $a$ and $b$ remain positive.
Each replaced larger value is replaced by a smaller positive difference.
$a=b$ always holds after at most one step.
The values are never changed during execution.

questions.explanation: The values remain positive, and the larger value gets smaller each time. This eventually reaches the base case $a=b$, but not necessarily after just one step.

questions.prompt: Which mapping of the base case and recursion step is correct?

options.text: Base case: $a<b$; step: add the two values.
Base case: $a=b$; step: replace the larger value with the difference and return to step 1.
Base case: read the input; step: output the result.
Base case: $a>b$; step: always stop immediately.

questions.explanation: The base case is the equality case. In the other cases, the larger value is reduced and the check is repeated.

questions.prompt: If $a\ne b$ in the Euclidean algorithm, it may stop with $a$ as the gcd.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The algorithm stops only at the base case $a=b$. If the values differ, further computation is needed first.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to place parentheses correctly in an `if` construct?

options.text: Without parentheses, all variables are defined automatically.
Otherwise, the compiler may group or interpret statements differently than intended.
Parentheses replace the `if` condition.
Parentheses make `readInt` read random values.

questions.explanation: Incorrectly placed parentheses can change which statements belong to a branch. As a result, the compiler may interpret the structure differently from what was intended.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish the types of finiteness? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: Dynamic finiteness is associated with termination of the execution.
Static finiteness means that every result is the same.
Dynamic finiteness means that only finitely many variables appear in `main`.
Static finiteness means that the description has finite length.

questions.explanation: Static finiteness concerns the length of the description; dynamic finiteness concerns behavior during execution. Identical results or the number of declared variables do not define these terms.

questions.prompt: What does the statement `result = x + 19;` mean in the variable model?

options.text: `result` is only checked for equality with `x`.
The statement ends the algorithm.
`x` is declared automatically and `result` is deleted.
The current value of `x` is used in the operation; the result is stored in `result`.

questions.explanation: The value of `x` can be used as an argument to the addition. The computed result is then stored in `result` by the assignment.
The condition $10>4$ is true, so the first branch runs and `result` receives the value $10-4=6$.

questions.prompt: Which mapping correctly connects each concept to execution?

options.text: Selection and iteration: both are types of comments.
Selection and iteration: both are used only for output.
Selection: choice based on a condition; iteration: repeated execution.
Selection: repeated execution; iteration: choice based on a condition.

questions.explanation: Selection chooses an execution path based on a condition. Iteration means repeatedly executing part of a program.

questions.prompt: Comments execute a program's commands repeatedly.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Comments explain a program. They do not execute commands repeatedly.

questions.prompt: When an `if` has multiple statements in each branch, which measures help make the intended structure clear? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: Group the statements in a branch into a block.
Omit blocks, because then all following statements automatically belong to the `if`.
Check which statements the compiler assigns to each branch.
Replace the condition with a comment.

questions.explanation: Blocks make the grouping of statements explicit. You should also check whether the branches are assigned as intended.

questions.prompt: You want to implement the requirement “fastest route without stairs” for an ordered list in MiniJava. Which strategy matches the algorithm described?

options.text: If two routes take the same time, always replace the current route with the new one.
Always choose the shortest route, even if it has stairs.
If all routes have stairs, automatically choose the fastest route with stairs.
Ignore routes with stairs and store a route as `best` if none has been selected yet or if it is faster.

questions.explanation: The requirement calls for a route without stairs. Therefore, routes with stairs are ignored, and a route is stored only if none has been selected yet or it is faster than the current choice.

questions.prompt: For a list of $n$ routes, the best route so far is stored and each new route is checked once. Which running time (Laufzeit) fits this approach?

options.text: $T(n)=n\in\Theta(n)$
$T(n)=n^2\in\Theta(n)$
$T(n)=1\in\Theta(1)$
$T(n)=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\in\Theta(n^2)$

questions.explanation: When the best route so far is stored, each new route is checked exactly once. Therefore, $T(n)=n\in\Theta(n)$.

questions.prompt:
A route planner should select a route with no stairs. If no available route meets this requirement, it should output “No suitable route.” Exactly two routes are available: Route A takes 6 minutes and has stairs; Route B takes 9 minutes and has stairs.

Statement: The planner should output Route A because it is the fastest available route.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Both available routes have stairs and therefore fail to meet the stated requirement. The planner should output “No suitable route,” not Route A.

questions.prompt: What value does the Euclidean algorithm return for $a=84$ and $b=30$?
questions.explanation: The differences produce $(84,30)\to(54,30)\to(24,30)\to(24,6)\to(18,6)\to(12,6)\to(6,6)$. The base case returns 6.
The inputs set `x=11` and `y=4`. Since $11>4$, the first branch is selected and $11-4=7$ is output.

questions.prompt: Which statements together provide a correct explanation of why the Euclidean algorithm is an algorithm in the sense described? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: For positive integers $a$ and $b$, it specifies a precise sequence of steps.
A finite description is not required for an algorithm.
At the base case, a value is returned as the greatest common divisor.
Termination depends on the values growing without bound.

questions.explanation: The algorithm specifies precise steps for the input and returns the gcd at the base case. A finite description is a property of algorithms, and the values do not grow without bound.

options.text: `x` may only have the value 0.
`result` was not defined before it was used.
`write` can only output variables that were read using `readInt`.
A variable must never be used in `write`.

questions.explanation: Variables declared inside `main` are not given a default value. Therefore, `result` must be defined before the call to `write`.

questions.prompt: Which combinations match the development and execution of a MiniJava program? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: `write` creates comments in the program.
Comments can explain the purpose of a program.
Blocks can group several statements in a branch.
`javac` compiles, and `java` runs the program.
`readInt` replaces the compilation process.

questions.explanation: Blocks structure statements, comments explain code, and `javac` and `java` are used for compilation and execution. `readInt` and `write`, in contrast, are input/output commands.

questions.prompt: A procedure has a finite description but does not terminate for a particular input. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It satisfies static but not dynamic finiteness.
It satisfies both forms of finiteness.
It satisfies neither form because the description is finite.
It satisfies dynamic but not static finiteness.

questions.explanation: The finite description satisfies static finiteness. Since the execution does not end, dynamic finiteness, or termination, is not satisfied in this case.
Since $2>5$ is false, `result` is first set to $5-2=3$. The next assignment changes it to $3+19=22$.

questions.prompt: Which statements connect MiniJava constructs to their roles? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: `if` allows a choice based on a condition.
A comment repeatedly executes the program part it describes.
An assignment changes the value stored in a variable.
A variable's value can be used as an argument to an operation.
`write` declares a new variable.

questions.explanation: Variable values can be used in operations, `if` implements selection, and an assignment updates a stored value. Comments and `write` do not have these roles.

questions.prompt: You are traveling through a city: your navigation system receives a starting point, destination, and traffic data, then calculates a route step by step. Which concept best describes this process?

options.text: Comment
Algorithm
Variable
Assignment

questions.explanation: An algorithm precisely describes process steps that produce a desired result from inputs. Here, the starting point, destination, and traffic data are the input, and the route is the output.

questions.prompt: A messaging app uses a key to convert a message into ciphertext according to fixed rules. Which concept is primarily involved?

options.text: Algorithm
Variable
Block
Recursion base case

questions.explanation: Encryption consists of a precise sequence of processing steps, so it is an algorithm. It processes the message and key as inputs and produces ciphertext as the result.

questions.prompt: You are testing a PIN checker: a PIN has exactly four digits, each digit can be from 0 to 9, and leading zeros are allowed. How many different PINs are there?
questions.explanation: There are 10 possibilities for each of the four digits: $10^4=10\,000$. The PIN checker can process this finite set of possible inputs with an algorithm.

questions.prompt: You are programming a Sudoku solver and considering the successful solution case: it tries numbers and calls itself again for the smaller remaining problem. When is a suitable base case reached?

options.text: Another number is entered in a cell.
The Sudoku is completely and validly filled in.
There is still an empty cell.
The next possible number is selected.

questions.explanation: In the successful solution case, the base case ends further calls once the goal is reached: the Sudoku is completely and validly filled in. The recursion step, by contrast, handles a smaller remaining problem.

questions.prompt: Which two everyday situations clearly illustrate conditional selection with `if`/`else`?

options.text: An upload is repeated until the server confirms receipt.
A variable is assigned the value `42`.
An ATM dispenses cash only when the PIN is correct; otherwise, it displays an error message.
A thermostat turns the heating on below a temperature threshold and off otherwise.

questions.explanation: With `if`/`else`, one path is chosen depending on a condition. The other examples represent iteration or assignment.

questions.prompt: A logic module has five independent yes/no inputs. How many rows does a complete truth table need to cover all possible input combinations?
questions.explanation: Each binary input doubles the number of combinations: $2^5=32$. The truth table therefore represents a finite function for all possible inputs.

questions.prompt: In an Excel-like spreadsheet, `x = 7` initially. You then set `x` to `26`. Which concept does this illustrate?

options.text: Recursion base case
Assignment
Termination
Selection

questions.explanation: An assignment changes the value stored in a variable: `7` becomes `26`. The variable serves as a named storage location.

questions.prompt: You simulate the subtraction-based Euclidean algorithm for $(a,b)=(15,6)$. How many recursion steps occur before the base case is reached?
questions.explanation: The pairs are $(15,6)\to(9,6)\to(3,6)\to(3,3)$. That is three subtractions; then $a=b$ and the base case ends the algorithm.

questions.prompt: Is this statement true? When `javac` translates a Java program into Java bytecode according to fixed rules, an algorithm is at work.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The translation follows a fixed sequence of processing steps; this sequence is an algorithm. The input is the Java program, and the output, if compilation succeeds, is Java bytecode.

questions.prompt: You want to reduce the fraction $84/30$ in an app. Which subproblem does the Euclidean algorithm solve directly?

options.text: Find the greatest common divisor of 84 and 30.
Read a PIN as input.
Find the shortest route between two places.
Encrypt a message.

questions.explanation: To reduce the fraction, you need the greatest common divisor: $gcd(84,30)=6$, so the fraction is divided by 6. The Euclidean algorithm finds this divisor through repeated steps that terminate.
